home.title: Fighting hate and disinformation online
home.description: HATEDEMICS is a platform that leverages artificial intelligence to analyze online content, enhance critical thinking, and train responses to hate speech.
home.networkDescription: An interactive map to observe the connections between channels, content, and dynamics related to hate and disinformation online. Discover what happens on the web, follow the flows, and identify the key nodes of toxic communication.
home.counterspeechDescription: Train your ability to respond to hate and disinformation content with targeted writing exercises. Learn how to use reliable sources to create solid arguments and develop your critical thinking to change the tone of online debate.
home.educationalDescription: Explore resources and educational materials to understand and counter online hate.
home.guideDescription: What to know before using the platform.

network.title: Network
network.description: The network shows the connections between the collected telegram channels. A channel is a node and it is connected to another channel if it “recommends” it. Recommendations are generated automatically by Telegram based on the channels' users overlap.

humanRights.title: Human Rights
humanRights.description: The fundamental human rights outlined by the United Nations in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights protect and uphold the dignity, equality, and freedom of all people. Some of them are listed below in a simplified version.
humanRights.objectives:
• Developing knowledge about human rights;
  • Rising awareness about connection between human rights and hate speech and disinformation;
  • Learning possible argument for reaction on hate speech and disinformation.
humanRights.task:
Form 11 groups. Each group picks up one card. Each group discusses the meaning of the human right written on their card. After 5 minutes, the first group explains what the right means to them and how it connects to hate speech. The teacher may add to their explanation if needed.
Then, the next group with the following card explains the meaning of their right and its connection to hate speech. Repeat this process until all groups have shared.

articles.title: Art. 1
articles.text: All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.

articles.title: Art. 2
articles.text: Everyone has the right to be treated in the same way, irrespective of race, colour, sex, language, religion, political opinion, property, birth, or other status.

articles.title: Art. 3
articles.text: Everyone has the right to life and to live in freedom and safety.

articles.title: Art. 5
articles.text: Everyone has the right to be free from torture and from inhuman and degrading treatment.

articles.title: Art. 7
articles.text: The law is the same for everyone.

articles.title: Art. 13
articles.text: Everyone has the right to live and travel freely within state borders.

articles.title: Art. 14
articles.text: Everyone has the right to go to another country and ask for protection if they are being persecuted or are in danger of being persecuted.

articles.title: Art. 16
articles.text: Everyone has the right to marry and have a family.

articles.title: Art. 18
articles.text: Everyone has the right to believe whatever they wish (including, but not confined to, religion).

articles.title: Art. 19
articles.text: Everyone has the right to say what they think and to give and receive information freely.

articles.title: Art. 29
articles.text: Everyone must respect the rights of others.

articles.title: Art. 30
articles.text: No-one has the right to take away any of these rights.

debunking.title: Debunking
debunking.description:
What is debunking: When some people think of a fact-checker, they only see a journalist who looks into a claim, checks it and confirms whether it is true or not, the debunking process. Nevertheless, fighting disinformation effectively nowadays takes much more than that: quickly detecting possible hoaxes before they go viral and affect more people; explaining that not everything is black or white, helping people to be well-prepared against falsehoods through Media Literacy or regulation; creating tools to make it harder for others to deceive us, or fighting together against manipulation: this is what we call pre-bunking.

What is a disinformation narrative: What disinformation creators want you to believe. When an idea is repeated many times, people tend to believe it. Also, one hoax can contain several narratives.
debunking.objectives:
• Debunk and learn about what disinformation narratives are. It's also a pre-bunking exercise: discover what disinformation narratives are and the most spread ones in your country.
  • Learn some debunk techniques in a guided way, and understand why critical thinking and identifying viral hoaxes is essential to fight disinformation narratives.
debunking.task: Simulate the actions of a fact-checker by selecting the most effective way to debunk a claimed event. Can you also identify the related disinformation narrative?

bias.title: Biases and fallacies
bias.description:
Logical fallacies associated with hate speech and disinformation

The content of hate speech and disinformation may sometimes look very convincing. This is because people who perpetuate hate speech often rely on logical fallacies – constructs hate groups use to justify their causes and their belief that people who come across this content would consider it as reasonable and truthful. Logical fallacies can use false premises, true premises but false conclusions, or true premises and conclusions but a false argument. Some fallacies are produced with the intention of deceiving or making misinformation viral.

There are many fallacies that show up in hate speech. Here are some of them:

Argumentum ad populum – a non-substantive way of arguing in which the speaker appeals to the tastes, preferences and prejudices of the crowd. Based on national egoism, instincts, stereotypes or prejudices, the speaker tries to win over the crowd to their thesis (e.g. The majority of people in our country thinks like this, so this is the way we should act);

Ipse dixit – the way of argumenting without providing a valid proof (e.g. the political party said it so it must be true);

A slippery slope fallacy – occurs when someone claims that a position or decision will lead to a series of unintended negative consequences (e.g. we cannot let the migrants stay in our country as they will bring their families here and have children, which will lead us to losing our jobs and the collapse of the social security system, and as a result we will be poor and lose control over our country);

Either-or fallacy – where someone claims there are only two ways of approaching the issue, while there are many other options (e.g. you can either vote for this party or live your life in constant danger);

Post hoc, ergo propter hoc – logical error in wrongly concluding that there is a causal connection between two events merely because one occurred before the other (e.g. Ever since we got a new maths teacher, I’ve been getting bad grades. She must be the reason I’m doing poorly);

Argumentum Ad Hominem – when someone attacks the person making an argument rather than the argument itself (e.g. Don't listen to Peter's opinion on the group project — he's lazy and never does anything right);

Cherry picking – when someone selectively presents evidence that supports their argument while ignoring or dismissing evidence that contradicts it (e.g. "Hate speech isn't harmful. Look at this one study that says it's just offensive, not dangerous" - while ignoring dozens of other studies showing the psychological and social harm of hate speech);

Appeal to tradition – when an argument assumes something is good or true simply because it is being traditionally done or believed, without considering whether it is still valid in the present context (e.g. In our school we have always had more men than women in the school council, and it always worked well).

Argument from anecdote – someone uses a single, often personal, experience or story to support a general conclusion or claim (e.g. I don't think hate speech leads to real harm. I’ve heard people make offensive jokes all the time, and no one I know has ever been seriously affected);

Ad ignorantiam fallacy – someone argues that a claim is true or false simply because it has not been proven the opposite (e.g. No one has ever proven that students cheat on online exams, so it must not happen).

Cognitive Biases

Our brain uses shortcuts to help us make quick decisions in everyday life. These shortcuts help us focus only on the most important information, so we don’t get overwhelmed by everything we see and hear. This makes the brain work more efficiently. However, the downside is that these shortcuts can sometimes lead us to make mistakes or misunderstand things because of our thinking (cognitive) biases.

We are all affected by cognitive biases in our decision-making process, and those who spread disinformation understand these biases very well. Here are some examples of cognitive biases:

Membership bias – tendency to favour own group over other groups;
Availability bias – tendency to rely on information that comes quickly to mind;
Causality bias – occurs when people believe that there is a relationship between events that are actually independent of each other;
Blind spot bias – the tendency to see oneself as less biased than other people;
Confirmation bias – tendency to search for, interpret, favour and recall information in a way that confirms prior beliefs;
Authority bias – tendency to be more influenced by the opinions of authority people.
bias.objectives:
• Develop awareness about social mechanisms, cognitive biases and logical fallacies
  • Develop critical thinking competence

Social mechanisms, cognitive biases and logical fallacies are factors which help hate speech and disinformation spread. By getting to know some of them, we can be more immune to them and be more critical to other forms of manipulation.
bias.task:
- Match the situation with the relevant logical fallacy / bias
- Is the situation an example of hate speech / disinformation / misinformation? If yes, why?

pairs.right: During a heated online discussion about immigration, a user posts: "Everyone knows that these people are dangerous and bring crime. Just look at how many people in our town agree with me. We need to get them out to protect our community."

During a community meeting about updating local school policies to be more inclusive of LGBTQ+ students, a long-time resident stands up and says: "For generations, we have taught that marriage is only between a man and a woman. This is how it has always been and how it should stay. Promoting these new ideas in our schools is an attack on our traditions and values."

During a public debate on refugee resettlement, a speaker points to a recent rise in unemployment that occurred shortly after a group of refugees arrived in the town. They declare, "Ever since they arrived, our unemployment rates have shot up. It's obvious they are taking all the jobs from hardworking local people."

During an online discussion about a recent crime reported in the news, a person writes, "As someone who has lived in this neighbourhood my whole life, I can tell you it's the new immigrants causing all the trouble. We 'originals' know what's really going on, and things were peaceful before they came."

During a heated debate about religious groups, a participant states, "Unlike those people, whose beliefs are full of prejudice and intolerance, I've examined my views objectively. My conclusion that their religion is inherently backward and dangerous isn't a bias; it's just an uncomfortable fact."

During a debate about allowing a new community center for a minority group, a speaker argues: "If we allow them to build this center, next they'll demand their own laws. Soon, they'll be taking over our neighbourhoods and imposing their culture on our children. We must stop this now, or we will lose our entire way of life."

bias.reflectionText:
Was it easy or difficult to match the situations and logical fallacies/bias?

Did you know some of them? Which? Which were totally new for you?

Can you provide concrete examples from your reality that represent some of those fallacies and biases?

Do you know any other examples of logical fallacies / bias?

How can the knowledge of those biases / logical fallacies help us in acting against hate speech and disinformation?

lateralreading.title: Lateral reading
lateralreading.description:
Lateral reading is a technique that allows us to quickly assess whether a web page's content comes from reliable sources and is based on quality data, references, and information.

In a research conducted by the Stanford History Education Group, educators discovered that it is an efficient way to assess the quality of an unfamiliar website.

This powerful strategy (used by fact-checkers) to evaluate information online involves not reading a website ‘vertically’, as if it were a printed document, but instead using a method called ‘lateral reading’.

This means analysing the webpage by opening several tabs to answer key questions about the content:
  • Who is the author of the content? Is it an expert source?
  • Can we find evidence? Is it based on facts and data?
  • Is it published by other reliable sources? What do they say about it?

In addition to the above key questions, the lateral reading technique invites us to promote critical thinking and go deeper by analysing other aspects of the content, such as:
  • Who funds or sponsors the site where the original piece was published?
  • What do other authoritative sources say about that site?
  • When you search for the topic of the original piece, are the top results from fact-checking organisations?
  • Have any questions been raised about other articles the author has written?
  • Does the information you find elsewhere contradict the original piece?
  • Are credible news outlets reporting on — or perhaps more importantly, not reporting on — what you are reading?

Lateral reading helps us better evaluate our sources of information — that is, to distinguish between truth and lies — and to consciously exercise our right to choose how we access information.
lateralreading.objectives:
• Learning about transparency and source credibility factors
  • Developing competence in identifying trustworthy sources of information
